result:
**On Dust**

Consider the dust mote. Before dismissing it as nothing—the residue of neglect spinning in a shaft of afternoon light—consider that it is older than your house, older than your street. Every speck drifting through a sunbeam may contain fragments of desert sand lifted by wind decades ago, volcanic ash from eruptions across oceans, pollen from forests you've never walked, skin cells shed by strangers now dead. Dust is memory made physical: the world reduced to particles fine enough to nearly forget gravity.

We fight dust endlessly. We wipe it from shelves, sweep it from corners, filter it from our air. Yet it returns with patient democracy, settling equally on palaces and porches. It is the great leveler that arrives before death does, softer and far less dramatic.

And here is the strangest part: we only see dust in certain light. A beam through a window reveals thousands of motes wheeling in slow chaos, but remove the slant of sun and the same air looks empty. It was never empty. We simply couldn't see.

Maybe that's worth carrying into ordinary days—that invisibility isn't absence. Most of what surrounds us goes unnoticed until some particular illumination catches it and makes it briefly luminous. People, probably. Ideas too. Everything suspended, drifting, composed of places we've never been, waiting patiently for the right angle of light to prove it was there all along.
